ops.title: Orchestrating fleet-wide changes: rules from the Jul 2026 swarm incident
ops.body:
# Orchestrating fleet-wide changes

Distilled from the Jul 17–26 2026 incident: a single-bug debugging session became a recursive 150-agent codex swarm (~1.8B tokens over 7 days) that cut ~15 daemonkit releases in 2 days, shipped three incompatible cc-pool store-schema epochs in 4 days, hard-cut the synckit state envelope and manifest schema with no migrations, wedged every machine's sync mesh, and recorded none of it. Recovery took a full coordinated stabilization pass (baseline v0.20.6, 12-repo repin, 10 releases, 2 machine cutovers).

## Orchestration shape

- **One orchestrator, bounded workflows.** Fan out via workflow scripts with explicit phases; never recursive self-spawning agents. Deciding next steps is never delegated downward — a lane that hits a shape-change stops and checks back with findings + options.
- **No unattended multi-day bypass sessions.** Every long-running pass has a human-visible record trail and check-back gates.
- **GitHub is the source of truth; re-verify at every dispatch point.** Clones, plans, and "known facts" go stale while other sessions work. Every lane fetches before acting and adopts work already done.
- **Record as you go.** The swarm's three schema cutovers had zero records; every remedy had to be re-derived from source days later. Each cutover, decision, and recipe goes to cc-notes when it happens, in the repo it belongs to.

## Releases

- **One release per coherent changeset.** Never N-per-day version churn.
- **Never ship a schema/protocol hard cut without**: a migration path (or an explicit, documented recreate procedure), a CHANGELOG entry, and an upgrade note. Three products violated this (cc-pool store epochs, synckit state envelope, synckit manifest model); two machines wedged for days. Fail-closed exactness (fingerprints, exact-match envelopes, exact-build wire handshakes) is good design *only* paired with a migration story — otherwise every partial upgrade is an outage.
- **Signing**: fleet release gates require the trusted key `F3299DE3FE0F6C3CF2B66BFBF7ECDD88A700D73A` with tagger `yasyfm@gmail.com`. Repo-default keys fail verify-tag-on-main, and the immutable-v*-tag rulesets make a wrong-key tag permanent — the remedies are cut-the-next-version or accept a missing release object (see note on daemonkit v0.20.6).
- **Converge in dependency order**: library baseline pin on every main (green CI) → releases for everything brew/plugin-distributed → machine upgrades. Cross-pin lockstep gates (e.g. cc-pool's suite-pins job tying Swift exactVersion to go.mod) mean a Swift-side pin left behind blocks a whole repo — sweep *all* pin surfaces (go.mod, Package.swift, Package.resolved, project.yml).
- **Enumerate downstreams from evidence, not memory** — the stabilization repin wave missed cookiesync, a 12th downstream, because the list came from a stale inventory.

## Daemons and machines

- **brew upgrade does not converge a running KeepAlive daemon.** A non-exiting process holds its old image indefinitely — including an *unlinked* image after the keg is deleted (synckit serve ran a deleted 0.21.0 binary for 6 days). daemonkit's StableProgram/drain-on-upgrade ownership (staged canonical executable under `~/.daemonkit/bin`, daemonkit-owned LaunchAgents) exists for exactly this; consumers must adopt it, and repair passes must lsof the *running* image, never trust the symlink.
- **Machine repair discipline**: read-only snapshot first; evidence-gated process kills (cmdline + PPID + lsof — circumstantial attribution killed nothing tonight only because the gate refused it); archive-never-delete for state and manifests; consumer-owned regeneration over hand-written schemas (fingerprinted manifests make hand-writing impossible by design); a verified-in-sandbox mechanical transformation is the only acceptable form of hand migration; verify by count sampling when log clocks skew; caffeinate remote machines and expect network death mid-pass (checkpoint reports, detached long steps, resumable staging).
- **Interactive credentials are user-gated.** Account re-auth (OAuth logins) cannot be delegated — plan repairs so everything else converges around that gap and the user does one batched re-auth pass.
ops.when: Before orchestrating any fleet-wide change: multi-repo releases or repins, schema/protocol changes, daemon upgrades, or machine convergence passes
